name: Lena Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two plastic injection presses making small car trim clips, pulling samples and gauging each first part after a mould change. My vocational certificate got me onto the line and eleven years taught me the sound of a clean cycle. I am an experienced operator, though the plant still pays me below the usual rate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mark cooks in a care home, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have less than a month saved and only a few similar factories nearby. I have never used AI; I keep a paper setup card and ask the setter before a difficult mould change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plastics crew that an AI office note does not remove a stuck part from a hot mould. I have never used an AI tool and will keep my paper setup card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the two presses well after eleven years and hold a vocational certificate, but the wage is low and the mortgage is due every month. Mark’s care-home kitchen pay is smaller, our two children need school costs, and less than a month is saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep gauging the first car trim clip after every changeover and take any paid Saturday shift offered. If a full month leaves money after essentials, I would pay a fresh extra amount against the mortgage, rather than call our existing cash new saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money even in a quiet AI world. A broken car could erase our whole reserve before the press changes at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which clip fault stops a run?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little fin of plastic at the edge means the mould has not closed cleanly. I stop the press and call the setter before boxes fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Saturday hours always be available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would accept them if offered, and extra mortgage payment would come only from actual new pay after bills. I cannot budget a shift that has not been posted.

say: I would tell the **plastics crew** a stuck hot mould still needs trained hands.
I would keep my **paper setup card** rather than use AI.
think: My **low wage** and mortgage already leave little spare.
Mark’s **smaller wage** and less than a month saved cannot cover a long stoppage.
do: Gauge **first trim clips** after changeovers and call the setter on bad edges.
Pay **extra mortgage principal** only from new surplus wages.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline bills and a fragile reserve.
S0.quote: A broken car could erase our whole reserve before the press changes at all.
fieldNote: Lena’s long experience and **vocational certificate** do not remove a real household cash squeeze.
Her extra debt payment depends on **actual new pay**, not an assumed overtime offer.

steps.text: Keep gauging first clips on the two presses
Pay extra mortgage principal only from actual new surplus pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that faster ordering must not turn mould cleaning into unpaid time. I would put the old and new setup records before our union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI planning might compress paid setup minutes, and robots could later lift the trim clips without a helper. I can run the presses, but a cut to my own hours would leave Mark’s kitchen wage far short of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log the next four paid changeovers and bring the numbers to the branch meeting. If two rosters cut my hours, we would cancel the children’s weekend club and I would look at posted nearby plastics jobs only where the wage meets our bills; I would not sign up for a screen course without an actual place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of anger at the idea of free work. The union can ask for records, but it cannot pay our mortgage for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show at the branch meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The start and finish times for each mould clean, and the paid minutes on my slip. I want a written rota with enough time to check the guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new planning screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI. I would ask for an in-person demonstration if the screen became part of my station, but watching it would not be training.

say: I would demand **paid mould cleaning** before faster schedules are accepted.
I would bring **setup records** to the union branch.
think: My **own hours** could shrink under tighter targets.
Mark’s **care-home wage** cannot meet the mortgage and our children’s school costs alone.
do: Log **four paid changeovers** and present them at a union meeting.
Cancel the **weekend club** after two reduced rosters.
Look for **posted nearby plastics work** only at bill-covering pay after cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, with anger at unpaid setup.
S1.quote: The union can ask for records, but it cannot pay our mortgage for us.
fieldNote: She uses a real **branch meeting** to seek paid safety time.
Her fallback is to **look at postings**, not claim an application or a training course already completed.

steps.text: Bring four paid mould-change records to union branch
Cancel children’s weekend club after two reduced rosters
Look for posted nearby bill-covering plastics work after cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line thinking AI might change orders in 2028 when I am forty five, while capable hands-on robots reach our presses around 2031 when I am forty eight. A robot arm needs a proven guard before anyone cuts a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most clip-ejection and box-filling hours to disappear when those robots work properly. Mark’s smaller wage, the mortgage and less than a month saved leave us no bridge for a long loss; I lie awake thinking of the children’s rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop optional spending and ask the manager for written staffing dates. If paid hours end, I would apply only for a posted reachable factory role with bill-covering pay and safe paid instruction; if no such opening exists, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment plan before arrears and take the union to the staffing meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a major likely wage loss. I can make those calls, but none guarantees a job before our next mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask to operate the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a paid supervised trial behind a tested guard. I would not touch controls without an offered paid practice place and a qualified safety lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a short payment change is possible if my shifts actually stop. I would bring the current wage slips and never assume the lender must agree.

say: I would separate **2028 ordering AI** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I would require a **guarded trial** before a robot replaces clip workers.
think: I expect **most ejection hours** to go after capable robots arrive.
Our **tiny reserve** and Mark’s smaller wage cannot bridge a long mortgage gap.
do: Cut **optional spending** and request written staffing dates.
Apply after **lost hours** only to posted reachable bill-covering work with paid safe instruction.
Ask the **lender** for a possible temporary plan if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: A robot arm needs a proven guard before anyone cuts a crew.
fieldNote: Lena expects **major hour loss** and says she lies awake over the house.
The trial is a **request to watch**; a new job and lender plan remain subject to posting, pay, safety and approval.

steps.text: Cut optional spending and request written staffing dates
Apply after lost hours to posted reachable bill-covering job with paid safe instruction
Ask lender for temporary mortgage plan if no adequate opening appears
Take staffing dates to union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight and capable press robots around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years gives the union time to insist that people learn on paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need every low-paid press hour at fifty one; a robot date does not clear the mortgage. I would consider a setter qualification only if it leads to a real local paid role rather than an unpaid classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current presses and put a fresh amount from full paid months against the mortgage after essentials. If the plant offers a fully funded practical setter course with paid time and a stopped-machine place, and a posted nearby role pays our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; I would ask the union to secure those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to ask for something specific. I would rather learn a mould change beside a fitter than pretend a video made me a setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the setter course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate a press, let me fit a mould and have me gauge the first part before restart. I need an actual workshop place and paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only unpaid study is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid press shift. Mark and I cannot spend our small reserve to train for a role that is not posted at a usable wage.

say: I would demand **paid practical learning** before 2034 robots enter the press area.
I would keep **2031 planning AI** distinct from physical work.
think: My **mortgage** still needs press wages at fifty one.
A **setter certificate** helps only with a real adequate local role.
do: Keep the **current presses** and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh surplus.
Enrol in **funded paid-time setter training** only with an offered stopped-machine place and posted bill-covering job.
Apply after **qualification** for that safe local role.
feel: **Anxious**, with a conditional paid route to test.
S3.quote: I would rather learn a mould change beside a fitter than pretend a video made me a setter.
fieldNote: Her resistance to AI permits **practical mechanical learning** when real wages and safe instruction are available.
The later **application** follows funded paid training and requires an offered place plus posted adequate local work.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal only from full-month surplus wages
Enrol in funded paid setter course if stopped-machine place and posted adequate job exist
Apply after qualification for posted local bill-covering setter job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, with capable press robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years is long enough for proper paid apprenticeships if management chooses to offer them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will be older, but the mortgage and our low wages do not disappear by calendar. I may still need press work at fifty six, and today’s tiny reserve makes a distant robot less important than the next paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep my two presses running and take actual overtime when offered, then bring paid-hour records to the branch. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare real rosters with local postings; after a sustained cut I would apply only for a posted bill-covering safe role, and ask the lender for a plan if no such wage appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our present money and uneasy about the distant press. I would rather hear the union argue over real hours than imagine a pension that has not been priced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work until 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there is safe paid work and our household still needs it. I cannot promise my health or a factory job thirteen years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the branch ask for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written paid training hours and a chance for experienced operators to apply for posted setter places. I would take my current rota, not a sales forecast.

say: I would ask for **paid apprenticeships** before 2039 press robots.
I would separate **2036 thinking AI** from later physical automation.
think: Our **mortgage and low wages** still matter today.
I may need **safe paid work** at fifty six without assuming a future role.
do: Keep **two presses** now and take offered paid overtime.
Apply after **sustained post-2036 cuts** only to posted bill-covering safe work.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills, with unease about distant robots.
S4.quote: I would rather hear the union argue over real hours than imagine a pension that has not been priced.
fieldNote: Her **baseline income pressure** persists through the long scenario.
She distinguishes **2026 shifts** from conditional post-2036 work requiring actual rosters and a posted adequate role.

steps.text: Keep press shifts and take paid overtime only when offered
Bring paid-hour records to union branch
Apply after sustained cuts to posted bill-covering safe local job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable press robots around 2031 could remove most clip-handling hours while our mortgage still needs both wages. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and posted local work at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the experienced operator while a robot learns the mould change. My children cannot eat a promise about future work.

headlineQuote: My children cannot eat a promise about future work.
portrait: **Lena**, 43, is an experienced injection-press operator with a vocational certificate and a paper setup routine.
Her **low pay**, care-home partner, two children, mortgage, tiny reserve and few local factories keep household money tight.
She has **never used AI** and presses her union for paid safe training and honest staffing dates.
Her **baseline anxiety** persists in the plateau; expected major hour loss makes fast robots alarming.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Lena’s clip-handling hours around 2031 before the household builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, paid safe practical training and posted bill-covering local jobs would help.
